summary: Teach three KS3 quantitative force laws (moments, fluid/hydraulic pressure, Hooke's Law) as one shared cognitive move: a measured force is linked to a second quantity (distance, area, or extension) through a fixed law. For levers and hydraulics, a force gained is paid for in extra distance moved — never 'something for nothing'. For a spring, force and extension are proportional up to the limit of proportionality. Build each law concrete-to-quantitative: predict on a felt, balanced setup, collect force/partner data pairs, then plot the straight line (or read the balance condition for moments) and name the equation and its gradient. For 12–14 year olds with secure multiplicative reasoning and graph-reading.
misconceptions: Calling a moment a 'turning force' — a moment is force × distance (units N·m), not a force; the wrong name hides the distance factor.
Confusing moment with momentum because the words sound alike — unrelated quantities.
Measuring the lever arm ALONG the arm rather than the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action, over-estimating angled moments.
Believing balanced moments alone mean the object is in equilibrium — it also needs zero resultant force (a balanced see-saw can still accelerate downward if unsupported).
Treating a lever or hydraulic as 'something for nothing' — not realising the multiplied force is paid for in extra distance moved.
Confusing force and pressure — thinking a heavier object always exerts more pressure, ignoring the area it is spread over.
Reading Hooke's Law as 'always proportional' — not realising it fails beyond the elastic limit where the spring deforms permanently and the graph curves.
Thinking pressure in a liquid acts only downward, rather than equally in all directions and normal to every surface, increasing with depth.

activities.title: Predict-then-measure on a balance beam
steps: Set up a metre-rule on a knife-edge pivot at its own balance point (centre of mass, usually near the 50 cm mark) so the rule's weight has no moment, with slotted masses that can hang at marked distances.
Before adding a lighter mass to balance a heavier mass placed near the pivot, predict WHERE the lighter mass must go and state why in words.
Slide the lighter mass and test; record the force (weight) and perpendicular distance on each side in a data table.
Repeat for several pairs, then check that clockwise moment (F × d) equals anticlockwise moment at balance.
Using an angled spanner on a nut, mark the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action and compare it to the length measured along the arm.
activities.insight: The turning effect is force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, not force alone; a small force far out balances a large force close in. Balance means equal moments on each side, not equal weights.

activities.title: The hydraulic trade: force up, distance down
steps: Use a syringe-and-tube hydraulic (small input syringe connected to a large output syringe) or an equivalent two-piston setup.
Predict whether pushing the small piston can lift a heavy load on the large piston, and whether you are 'getting force for free'.

Press the small piston and observe the large piston rise; read or compute the pressure (force ÷ area) on each side and confirm it is approximately equal (friction in real syringes causes small differences).
Track and compare how far the small piston moves versus how far the large piston moves.
State the trade: force is multiplied, but the small piston travels a long way while the big one barely moves, so work in ≈ work out — energy is conserved.
Relate the confined-fluid pressure to atmospheric pressure — the pressure caused by the weight of the air above, acting on all surfaces — and note how atmospheric pressure decreases with height.
activities.insight: Pressure is transmitted equally through a confined fluid (pressure = force ÷ area), so a small force on a small area lifts a large load on a large area — but the multiplied force is paid for in extra distance moved. Nothing comes for free. Atmospheric pressure is the separate everyday pressure of the air column, which decreases with height.

activities.title: Build Hooke's Law from a spring and find the elastic limit
steps: Hang slotted masses one at a time on a spring beside a ruler, recording applied force and extension for each load in a table.
Plot force against extension and check that the points fall on a straight line through the origin.
Read the gradient and name it as the stiffness/spring constant k, computing k = F ÷ x for several points to confirm it is constant in the linear region.

Keep loading beyond the linear region; note the point where the straight line bends (the limit of proportionality) and test whether the spring returns to its original length when unloaded (it does not once the elastic limit is passed).

Mark the limit of proportionality (where the line stops being straight) on the graph and state that Hooke's Law holds only up to that point; note that the elastic limit, beyond which the stretch is permanent, is at or just beyond it.
activities.insight: Extension is directly proportional to applied force up to the limit of proportionality (F = kx), with gradient k being the stiffness; beyond it the graph curves, and past the elastic limit (at or just beyond it) the deformation becomes permanent. Hooke's Law is a special case, not an always-true rule.

activities.title: Live 'force-trade bench' — isolate the proportional partner
steps: Use an interactive model with three swappable rigs (balance beam, two-piston hydraulic, loaded spring) that recompute as one quantity is changed.

On the balance rig, drag a hanging mass left/right and watch the moment readout (F × d) update on each side, with the bar snapping level the instant clockwise = anticlockwise; slide the same mass outward to see the rule 'win' the turn without added weight.

On the hydraulic rig, press the small piston, watch an identical pressure value on both sides and two force/area readouts, then watch a distance tracker show the small piston travelling far while the big one barely moves.

On the spring rig, hang masses to plot the force–extension point live, drawing the straight line whose gradient is k, then load past the elastic limit to watch the line bend and the spring stay stretched.

On the moments and hydraulic rigs, use the 'freeze the force, vary only the partner' toggle to isolate the effect of distance or area while the force stays fixed; on the spring rig, add force in equal steps and watch extension grow in equal steps within the linear region (up to the limit of proportionality), since there force and extension are locked together by k and cannot be varied independently.
activities.insight: Each law is a live proportional relationship: change one quantity and the partner recomputes. On the moments and hydraulic rigs, freezing the force while varying only distance or area isolates that factor's effect; on the spring, force and extension co-vary through the fixed k, so adding force in equal steps reveals the proportional extension directly.

activities.title: Consolidate and self-check the three laws
steps: Place a mass on a drawn or modelled rule to make it balance, justifying the position with F × d on each side.
Complete the relationships in writing: moment = force × perpendicular distance; pressure = force ÷ ___ (area); F = k × ___ (extension).

Sort described situations into 'Hooke's Law holds' versus 'beyond the limit of proportionality', and identify on a given force–extension graph the point where the line stops being straight (the limit of proportionality).
Order a set of springs by stiffness using their force–extension gradients.

Answer the probe questions in writing: where to push a heavy door and why (near the hinge or far edge); whether a hydraulic car jack gives energy for free and what is traded; how to find the spring constant and the elastic limit on a graph; which of a short or long spanner turns a stiff bolt more easily and why.
activities.insight: The learner can state and apply each law, read the law off a graph or diagram, explain the force-for-distance trade shared by levers and hydraulics, and explain the force–extension proportionality of springs, rather than treating them as unrelated formulas.

activities.title: Reference diagrams for naming and error pre-emption
steps: Study a labelled balanced-rule diagram and tag the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action on each side.
Study a two-piston hydraulic diagram with equal-pressure arrows and label where force is multiplied and where distance is traded.
Study an annotated force–extension graph: straight line through the origin, gradient k, and the limit of proportionality flagged where the line bends (with the elastic limit at or just beyond it).
Study a pressure-with-depth diagram with arrows acting normal to all surfaces and longer at greater depth.
For each diagram, write the quantity each label represents and the common error it guards against (perpendicular distance vs along-arm; force vs pressure; proportional vs beyond-limit).
activities.insight: Correct naming of parts — perpendicular distance, equal pressure, elastic limit, pressure acting normal to all surfaces — anchors the vocabulary and pre-empts the perpendicular-distance and force-vs-pressure errors.

checkQuestion: Two children sit on a see-saw. A heavy child sits close to the pivot; a lighter child sits far out on the other side — and it balances. How can the lighter child balance the heavier one? What makes the two sides equal?
checkAnswer: The turning effect (moment) is force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, not force alone. The lighter child's smaller weight multiplied by their LARGER distance from the pivot gives the same moment as the heavier child's larger weight multiplied by their SMALLER distance. Balance means equal moments on each side, not equal weights.
